mechanics.title: The day has a shape: sales are lost by the hour, not by the month
mechanics.playerDecision: How many people stand at the bar in each part of the day (peak_schedule lever, staff count), whether to cap order-ahead in the rush, how long to stay open.
mechanics.engineMath: Split the day's demand by extra.hourCurve for the block type. For each hour: bar capacity = baristas on the bar x 25 orders an hour (30 drinks an hour / 1.2 drinks an order), times the menu_size capacity effect. Served = min(demand, capacity); the surplus is not simply lost: it stands in line, and extra.queue.walkAwayByPeopleAhead decides how many leave (mechanic queue_walkaway). Monthly totals are the sums. With this the engine's flat rule (1,700 orders per person a month) stops hiding the 8am problem: at 200 orders a day the 8am hour brings 28-36 orders against 25 from one barista, while 3pm brings 14.
fieldsNeeded: staff schedule: people on the bar by daypart (open, rush, midday, afternoon, close)

mechanics.title: People count the line, not the minutes
mechanics.playerDecision: Nothing new to click: it is what punishes a thin bar at 8am. The player's moves are the rush schedule, the menu size, order-ahead with capped slots, and a second register.
mechanics.engineMath: In each hour, people ahead in line = max(0, arrivals - capacity) carried from the previous quarter-hour. Each arriving customer leaves with the probability in extra.queue.walkAwayByPeopleAhead (0 up to three people ahead, 5% at four to five, 15% at six to eight, 30% at nine to twelve, 50% beyond). Office commuters use the next step up of the table: they are on a clock. Those who leave follow the engine's existing rule: half try a neighbor with room. Those who stay but wait more than six minutes feed slow_service_reviews. Phone orders do not see the line, but each one adds a drink to the bar's queue: uncapped, they lengthen the visible wait for walk-ins (handoff_pileup).

mechanics.title: A visible star rating, earned review by review
mechanics.playerDecision: How to treat the listings (reviews lever), and whether to take the shortcuts: buy reviews, or reward good ones.
mechanics.engineMath: Keep two numbers per shop: reviewCount and ratingAverage (1-5), shown rounded to half stars. Each month about 1 order in 150 leaves a review (my assumption: 40 a month at 6,000 orders). The month's reviews average: 4.4 base, +1.5 x (quality - 0.5), -0.6 if the month had slow_service_reviews, -0.4 if a B or C hangs in the window, -0.3 after a price_step_backlash, +0.12 if the owner replies to reviews. ratingAverage moves toward it by reviewsThisMonth / reviewCount, so a new shop's rating swings and an old shop's barely moves. Demand multiplier for people who do not know the shop yet (newcomer share by segment): 1 + 0.07 x (displayed stars - 4.0), and an extra 0.93 while the displayed rating is under 4.0. Regulars ignore the stars. Bought reviews add 10 five-star reviews a month and open the fake_reviews trail; when found, the platform removes them and shows a warning for 90 days (the 90 days are a game value). In the engine's present model the same thing is carried by reputation with weight 0.09 (see market.note).

mechanics.title: The letter in the window sells or repels
mechanics.playerDecision: After a re-inspection that ends in a B or C: post the grade; or post 'Grade Pending' and contest the violations at the city tribunal; or (shortcut) take the card down.
mechanics.engineMath: Compute the letter from the open violation trails with the pack's extra.inspectionPoints (under 14 points A, 14-27 B, 28 or more C). Demand multiplier while the card hangs: A 1.00, Grade Pending 0.98, B 0.95, C 0.88 (extra.ratingModel.letterGrade), applied to newcomers and halved for regulars. Contesting: the shop posts Grade Pending until the hearing (about a month in the game); at the hearing each violation the player has actually fixed is dismissed and the points are recounted; if the score drops under 14 the shop gets its A, otherwise the B or C goes up and the fines stand. Hiding the card: no demand loss, but the next inspection or a neighbor's complaint adds grade_card_not_posted ($500). The grade is redone at the next cycle: 150-210 days after a B, 90-150 after a C.

mechanics.title: Five kinds of customer, each with its own week, clock and patience
mechanics.playerDecision: No new control: the player reads the mix on the place card before signing the lease and then tunes hours, schedule, laptops, entry price and listings to the people who are actually there.
mechanics.engineMath: Each place gets a block type from its anchors (office within 250 m: office; college within 400 m: campus; museum, plaza or hotel cluster: tourist; otherwise residential) and with it a segment mix (extra.guestSegments.mixByBlock). Daily demand = sum over segments of share x weekday profile x month profile x event multipliers that name the segment. Each segment carries its own seat use (remote workers 1.0, commuters 0.1), ticket, price sensitivity, patience in line and share of newcomers. Effects: an office block earns its week Tuesday to Thursday and nothing on Sunday; a campus block loses 12% in summer; a tourist block lives on the map rating; a residential block lives on regulars, who forgive a line but notice every price change.
fieldsNeeded: event effects that can name a segment

mechanics.title: Every channel keeps a different share of the dollar
mechanics.playerDecision: Which channels to open: order-ahead, a basic or promoted delivery listing, catering; whether to charge more on the apps than at the counter.
mechanics.engineMath: Revenue is recorded by channel. For each channel: contribution = sales x (1 - 0.28 cost of goods - channelTakes) - packaging. channelTakes comes from extra.channels: counter 4.1%, own order-ahead 6.8%, app pickup 9%, basic delivery 23%, promoted delivery up to 43%, catering marketplace 18%. Delivery tickets are larger (two drinks, a pastry) and the player may set an app price up to 15% above the counter price, which most restaurants do; a higher app price lowers app orders with the same elasticity. Delivery and order-ahead load the bar in the rush like any other order (hourly_peak) but need no seat. The city's caps bound what an app may take; an 'enhanced' plan is the player's choice, never a default. This replaces the fixed monthly costs used as a stand-in by the delivery_apps, order_ahead and catering levers.

mechanics.title: A rival opening or closing is announced, and it is not the end
mechanics.playerDecision: What to change in the month between the announcement and the opening: entry price, loyalty, beans, hours, a seasonal drink.
mechanics.engineMath: Chains and carts are non-playing rivals placed by the city deck on real vacant doors, announced a month ahead. A rival carries a type (chain, discount app chain, small-format chain, cart), a price index (chain 0.9, discount 0.6 during its opening quarter, cart 0.5) and the segments it pulls (commuters and students first, regulars last). In the footfall model it joins the split of passers-by with its own weight: 1.0 for a chain in its first six months (curiosity plus opening offers), 0.5 afterwards (the keen-cray staticWeight). The hit on a player's shop is larger the more its quality and price resemble the rival's: a differentiated shop (quality above 0.6) loses about a third as much. When a rival closes, its share is released over two months and split by attractiveness; a shop at capacity gets nothing. Planning size: -7% for six months when a chain opens within 250 m, +6% when one closes.

mechanics.title: Regulars are built slowly and lost one disappointment at a time
mechanics.playerDecision: Whether to spend on getting first visits (opening offer, listings, a seasonal drink) or on second visits (loyalty, the same barista, speed).
mechanics.engineMath: Split each segment's customers into regulars and newcomers. Regulars: a stock that grows each month by newcomers x conversion and shrinks by churn. Conversion from first visit to regular: 30% at average quality (range 20-45% with quality and loyalty); churn of regulars: 4% a month at rest, +10 points in a month with slow_service_reviews, +5 after price_step_backlash, +15 when a shift lead or senior barista leaves (task D05). Regulars buy 2-4 times a week and bring a newcomer now and then (0.05 a month each). Newcomers are driven by footfall, the map rating and the letter grade; regulars by none of those. This is the engine's 'awareness' ramp with a cause: a new shop starts with no regulars, which is why month one sells a third of month six; and a bought shop keeps the regulars only while it keeps what they came for. At steady state regulars should give 55-65% of orders.

mechanics.title: Customers remember last month's price
mechanics.playerDecision: How fast to raise prices: in one jump or in small steps, and whether to keep one cheap item on the board.
mechanics.engineMath: The engine's reference price is fixed at $8.50. Make it move: fairPrice rises 4% a year with the street (menu_prices_drift_up). Each shop also has a remembered price: last month's price for its regulars. A rise of up to 4% within a month costs only the ordinary elasticity; above that, regulars churn faster (price_step_backlash: 3% of demand for two months, a quarter-star less in that month's reviews). A cut is noticed slower than a rise: half the elasticity in the first month. A value item (value_anchor) lowers the price sensitivity of students and commuters by a third because the board shows a number they accept. A card surcharge counts as a price rise of its size for card payers.
fieldsNeeded: threshold and penalty values in extra

mechanics.title: A monthly pass: cash up front, margin at the mercy of the heaviest users
mechanics.playerDecision: Whether to sell a pass, at what price, and with what cap.
mechanics.engineMath: A pass is sold to regulars: price P a month for up to C drip coffees. Take-up: 5% of regulars at P = $45, C = 30, falling with price. A holder drinks min(C, 22) cups a month on average instead of 12, and buys food on one visit in four. Shop's month per holder: +P cash on day one, -cups x $0.80 ingredients and cup, +extra food margin; the list-price sales they would have made anyway (12 x $3.75 = $45) are gone. So a $45 pass with a 30-cup cap is roughly neutral on coffee and earns on food and on the habit; an uncapped pass loses on the top tenth of users. The cash arrives before the coffee is poured, which helps a thin month and is a liability on the books.
fieldsNeeded: lever with a price and a cap (two numbers), not just options
